name: v1.3.1 — the version string v1.3.0 forgot
body:
No behaviour change, no new code. v1.3.0 was tagged without the version bump that should have preceded it, so the tree it points at carries `__version__ = "1.2.0"`.

That string is not decoration. `USER_AGENT` is built from it and sent on every request, to targets and infrastructure alike — so v1.3.0 introduced itself as **`secscan/1.2.0`** to every host it scanned, and `pip show` agreed. An operator who read that header and went looking for the release notes matching the traffic they saw would have been reading about the wrong version. The file that holds the string makes the argument itself: a scanner that announces itself has to announce itself correctly or the courtesy is worth nothing.

**v1.3.0 is superseded, not replaced.** Its tag stays where it is and its notes describe its contents correctly — exit code `3`, the POST probes that never left the process, the CI gate on the active tier, the floors denominator, the hostname check that accepted a bare dot. Moving a published tag would erase the defect for anyone who already fetched it, and a version number that changes meaning after the fact is not a version number. Same precedent as v1.1.0 → v1.1.1.

Still wrong, and measured rather than suspected:

- The report derives *"active traffic was sent"* from which scanners were **selected**, not from requests actually **made**. A run that reaches nothing — every connection refused, exit `3` — still reports `sent_active_traffic: true`.
- The open-redirect check's 3xx status guard can be deleted outright and the new CI gate stays green, because no route in that gate returns a `200` carrying a `Location` header. The gate is real and it caught eight seeded mutations; that one assertion is not load-bearing yet.
- There is no way to ask the scanner its version. No `--version` flag, and `--help` does not print one — the only channels are the `User-Agent` header and `pip show`. The thing that went wrong here is not directly observable from the CLI that shipped it.

446 tests.

name: v1.3.0 — the active tier actually sends its probes
body:
> **Superseded by [v1.3.1](https://github.com/BU1lDR/security-scanner/releases/tag/v1.3.1).** This release was tagged without its version bump, so the tree it points at carries `__version__ = "1.2.0"` — which means it sends `secscan/1.2.0` in the `User-Agent` header to every host it scans, and `pip show` reports 1.2.0. Everything described below is accurate and unchanged. Use v1.3.1: the same code, with the version it claims. The tag is left where it is on purpose rather than moved.

The active tier's POST probes never left the process: a `list` handed to httpx's `data=` built a sync byte stream that `AsyncClient` refused, and a bare `except` swallowed it. Three checks against every form parameter on a target reported clean having sent nothing. 446 tests had agreed it was fine.

**The fix that matters is not the encode change — it is that CI now re-proves the whole active tier on every push** against a deliberately-flawed loopback site using matched pairs: every check gets one flawed route and one guarded route, asserted as exact set equality. A false positive fails the same assertion as a false negative.

Also in this release:
- **Exit code `3`** — "we could not look" no longer shares a code with "there is nothing wrong"
- A dot is not a hostname; target text bounded where it arrives
- Dependency floors reported "all 6 floors clean" over a `pyproject` declaring seven
- Test count now checked against the repo front page, not just `decisions.md`

Verify it yourself: clone, `pytest`, then run the scanner against your own staging target.

name: v1.2.0 — the scanner stops flagging itself, and discloses active traffic
body:
This release is mostly about the scanner telling the truth about itself: it no longer reports its own rule definitions as vulnerabilities, it now records in the report which scanners ran and whether any of them sent attack traffic, and a config file with a misspelt key is now an error instead of a setting that is silently ignored. The dependency floors were also raised off versions with known advisories against them. Nothing in the scanning surface was removed, and `requires-python` is still `>=3.11`.

## Fixed

**The SAST rule pack detected itself.** Scanning this project's own `./src` reported seventeen findings, sixteen of which were the rules matching their own text — the pattern for `eval\s*\(` matching the string literal `"Use of eval() on a dynamic value"`, the pattern for `shell=True` matching a sentence in a comment explaining why `shell=True` lines matter. The matcher worked on raw lines, so it had no way to distinguish a call from the same name quoted in a string or written in a comment. It now asks Python's own `tokenize` for the column ranges of every COMMENT and STRING token and drops a sink match that starts inside one. Three behaviours were kept deliberately, each with a test: secret rules are exempt, because a hardcoded credential is always inside a string literal and this guard would suppress every true positive that class exists to find; `eval("1 + " + user_input)` still reports, because the `eval(` is code and only the argument is a literal; and a file `tokenize` cannot read gets no guard rather than no scan, because a false positive costs a reviewer a minute and a false negative is the thing the tool exists to prevent.

**An active scan that found nothing looked exactly like a passive one.** A config file setting `dast.active.enabled` and `scope.authorized_ack` fully enables the intrusive checks while the command on screen is a bare `secscan https://host/`. The authorization gate itself was sound, but nothing recorded that attack-shaped requests had been sent: no flag in shell history, no line on stderr, nothing in the report. `ScanReport` now carries `scanners_run` and `active_scanners_run`, populated by the engine from its own selection rather than from what produced findings — a check that ran and found nothing still sent the requests. All three renderers disclose it: terminal and HTML print a line directly under the target, and JSON gains a `scan` block with `scanners_run`, `active_scanners_run` and `sent_active_traffic`. Whether a scanner counts as active is read from `cls.requires.active`, the same field the gate reads, not from a name suffix.

**A misspelt config key was accepted and ignored.** `exclude_dir` instead of `exclude_dirs` merged in beside the real key and did nothing, so the directory you asked to skip was scanned and the report filled with findings in third-party code you do not own. `per_host_rate` instead of `per_host_rps` left the target being hit at the default rate while the file on disk said otherwise. These are the settings whose only purpose is to bound what this tool does to a machine that is not yours, so a silent no-op is the wrong failure. `Config.load` now refuses an unknown key, names it, and suggests the nearest real one. Settings with closed sets are checked too, and one of those failed in the worst available direction: `dast.active.checks` was filtered against the known-check table, so `["xss-reflcted"]` selected nothing — the active tier ran, tried no checks, and returned an empty result that reads like a clean bill of health on an authorized test.

## Added

**`docs/configuration.md`** documents all 31 settings with their defaults. `--config PATH` had been in `--help` since the CLI existed, and the only listing of what belonged in the file was a namespace declaration for implementers, with bare key names and one setting missing entirely. The test suite now asserts the document and the defaults match in both directions — no setting without a row, no row without a setting — because the second direction is what catches a rename that leaves its old documentation confidently in place. The document also warns, at length, about putting `authorized_ack` in a file: it is the same legal assertion as typing `--i-am-authorized`, but it does not appear in the command you ran.

**`tools/check_self_scan.py`**, which scans this project with itself and requires both zero SAST findings against `./src` and exit 1 on a planted `eval(request.body)`. Both directions, because a scanner that reports nothing passes the first check alone and one that reports everything passes the second alone. It replaces a CI step that asserted `secscan ./src` exits 1 — which pinned the sixteen false positives as the expected result, so fixing them would have turned CI red.

**A socket-blocked second test pass.** The README's claim that no test touches the network is now checked rather than asserted: CI runs the whole suite again with `--disable-socket --allow-hosts=127.0.0.1,::1`. The loopback allowance is there because `asyncio` opens a socketpair for its own wakeup; blocking that would fail tests for reasons unrelated to the claim. Both halves were measured — the suite passes with sockets off, and a test opening a real connection to `api.osv.dev` fails under the same flags. It runs as a separate pass rather than a permanent `addopts` entry, because under those flags a test that starts reaching out fails with a pytest-socket error rather than a connection error, which is confusing to debug locally. `pytest-socket>=0.7` is a new dev dependency.

**`tools/check_floors.py`**, which asks OSV about every `>=` floor in `pyproject.toml`. It runs weekly, on demand, and on pushes that touch the floors — not on every commit, because its answer depends on what OSV published today rather than on what the commit changed, and a check that reddens an unrelated pull request the morning a new advisory lands is one contributors learn to ignore. It is stdlib-only, so it does not need the package installed to audit that package's install metadata.

## Changed

Dependency floors were raised to the lowest version OSV reports nothing against, each queried rather than guessed:

- `cryptography>=42` → `>=50`. Version 42.0.0 is installable, and asked on 20 September 2026, OSV returns fifteen records against it — nine distinct flaws once each CVE's GHSA and PYSEC copies are merged, four of them HIGH. 50 is the lowest version OSV reported nothing against, and is also where CVE-2026-69247 (a Bleichenbacher oracle in PKCS#7 EnvelopedData decryption, introduced after 42) is fixed.
- build requirement `setuptools>=61` → `>=83`, which admitted CVE-2024-6345 (code execution through the package-index download path) and CVE-2025-47273 (path traversal).
- dev `pytest>=8` → `>=9.0.3`, for CVE-2025-71176.

`httpx`, `beautifulsoup4` and `packaging` came back clean at their existing floors and were left there, because raising a floor that does not need it only costs users compatibility. Nothing anyone installed was actually vulnerable — every environment resolved well above these floors — which is why the old floors survived the whole life of the project, and is not a defence: a floor is a published claim that the named version is a supported install, and this tool's own SCA scanner would flag one like that in someone else's manifest.

Two numbers in that first bullet are worth separating, because the first version of `check_floors.py` did not. Fifteen is a count of OSV *records* and nine is a count of flaws; OSV publishes one record per source database, so a single CVE arrives as a GHSA and a PYSEC entry that alias each other. The script reported all fifteen until the same commit that raised the floors taught it to merge aliases, which is the deduplication the scanner has always done in `_cluster_vulns`. Any count of advisories is also OSV's to change without anyone here touching anything — which is the whole reason this check runs on a timer, and why the figures above carry the date they were asked on.

## Upgrading

This is a minor bump rather than a patch for one reason: a config file that loaded under v1.1.1 may now be a hard error. If you have a `--config` file, check its keys against [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) before upgrading. The error names the offending key and suggests the nearest real one, so the fix is usually a one-character edit. Reports gained a field; the JSON `scan` block is additive, and it is omitted entirely when nothing was recorded rather than emitted as `"sent_active_traffic": false`, so a pipeline gating on that key gets a missing key it has to handle rather than a default it will not question.

## Notes

The inert-span guard is Python-only, because `tokenize` is. A JS sink inside a string still reports, so the JS rules keep exactly the precision they had. On Python 3.11 an f-string is a single STRING token, so `f"{eval(x)}"` is a false negative there; from 3.12 the replacement field is correctly seen as code. Key names are validated in config files, not value types — `per_host_rps = "fast"` still gets through and fails later in the rate limiter.

## Install

Python 3.11 or newer.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate       # on Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e .
secscan path/to/code
```

Or without installing:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m scanner.cli path/to/code
```

Tests, including the offline check:

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python -m pytest -q
python -m pytest -q --disable-socket --allow-hosts=127.0.0.1,::1
```

name: v1.1.1 — SAST no longer scans venv/ and __pycache__/
body:
A bug-fix release. v1.1.0 was tagged before the fix below landed, so the SAST scanner in v1.1.0 walks `venv/` and `__pycache__/` and reports findings in third-party code you do not own. The v1.1.0 tag has not been moved — published tags stay where they are — so this is the release that contains the fix. If you are on v1.1.0, move to v1.1.1.

## Fixed

The list of directory names pruned from a local walk existed in three places and they disagreed. `core/config.py` defaults listed five names; `sast/scanner.py` and `sca/scanner.py` each held their own seven-name copy that added `venv` and `__pycache__`.

Because a `Config` always has the defaults merged in, `cfg.get("sast.exclude_dirs", ...)` never reached the SAST scanner's own fallback: the five-name list won every real run, and the seven-name copy beside it was dead code that read as though it were in force. SCA was not better but worse — `sca.exclude_dirs` was absent from the defaults entirely, so its seven-name fallback *was* the one in force. The result was that SAST pruned five directory names while SCA pruned seven, in the same scan, and both files looked like they agreed. Point the scanner at a project laid out the ordinary way — a virtualenv in the working directory — and SAST scanned the whole virtualenv.

SAST now prunes the same seven names SCA already did, so a default scan of a code path reports on your source and not on your dependencies' source. There is one `DEFAULT_EXCLUDE_DIRS` in `core/config.py`, both scanners import it as their fallback, and `sca.exclude_dirs` is written into the defaults rather than left to a fallback, so the default and the fallback can no longer drift apart. If your config file sets `sast.exclude_dirs` explicitly, nothing about your runs changes.

Two tests cover this, both of which fail if it is reintroduced. The first plants the same secret in `venv/`, `.venv/`, `__pycache__/` and `src/` and asserts only `src/` is reported; it is the first test in that file to build a `Config` the way a real run does, which is why the default-config path — the only path a user hits — had been the untested one. The second asserts by identity that both scanners' fallbacks are the defaults' list.

## Added

CI now checks the test count quoted in `decisions.md` against what pytest collects, and fails with both figures and the line to edit. That figure goes stale whenever tests are added, and it did on the commit immediately before this check was written: `decisions.md` said 355 while pytest collected 357. The same number is also written down in two other repositories that CI here cannot see, so the failure message names them. A number that goes stale whenever the project improves cannot be kept correct by intending to keep it correct. The check needs no network and no state beyond a collection pass.

## Notes

Python 3.11 or newer. There is no package on an index; install from a clone with `pip install -e .`, which provides the `secscan` command, or run it in place with `PYTHONPATH=src python -m scanner.cli path/to/code`.

The scanner reports its own version in its User-Agent, so scans from this release identify themselves as `secscan/1.1.1`.

name: v1.1.0 — a silent SCA gap is now a finding
body:
This release exists because v1.0.0 could not be trusted to tell you when it had not looked. Point v1.0.0 at a project whose dependencies live in `composer.json`, `go.mod`, `pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, a `.csproj`, or a Poetry-style `pyproject.toml`, and the SCA pass read none of it and said "No findings", exit 0 — the same output a genuinely clean project produces. This version reports what it could not read, fails on a target path that does not exist instead of reporting success, and stops sending an unrelated stranger's GitHub URL to every host it scans.

## Fixed

- **SCA no longer answers "nothing found" when it could not look.** Four paths reached no vulnerability lookup and stayed silent, each producing the same empty SCA section a clean project produces: a manifest in an ecosystem this scan does not cover, a project with no recognized manifest at all, a dependency pinned to a range rather than an exact version, and dependencies resolved and then abandoned because no HTTP client was available. The first three now produce an explicit finding naming what went unread; the fourth raises a recorded scan error naming the packages that were resolved and never checked. The worst case was a Poetry `pyproject.toml`: the filename is supported, so it parsed without complaint and resolved to zero dependencies. That is now detected by content rather than by name.
- **Gaps inside a covered ecosystem are worded differently from gaps outside one.** A `poetry.lock` or `Pipfile.lock` holds PyPI packages, so "this scan does not check PyPI" would be false about a tool that does. The finding says only the declaration format was not read.
- **A mistyped target path now fails.** `secscan ./scr`, one keystroke off `./src`, used to scan a directory that does not exist, find nothing, print a report and exit 0 — in a pipeline, a green tick meaning the scan never ran. Unrecognized targets now exit 2, the code `decisions.md` D14 assigns to the tool itself erroring, which `cli.py` had already read as covering a bad target with nothing raising to make it happen. The message names the resolved absolute path, because the usual cause is being in a different working directory than you thought, and echoing the relative path back does not show you that.
- **The User-Agent is correct and comes from one place.** The default was `secscan/0.1 (+https://github.com/security-scanner)`, sent on every request to targets and to infrastructure alike. The version was two releases behind, and that URL is a real, unrelated GitHub account with no connection to this project — so the operator of a scanned host, reading the header to find out who was knocking, was pointed at a stranger's profile. It is now `secscan/1.1.0 (+https://github.com/BU1lDR/security-scanner)`, composed once in `src/scanner/__init__.py`; `core/http.py` and `core/config.py` import it and `pyproject.toml` reads the version from it, so a release bump is one line in one file.
- **The terminal report no longer implies a flag that does not exist.** Fixes classified as safe were tagged "auto-applicable", which sent readers looking for an apply command. The tag now reads "safe to apply as-is" — a statement about the change, not about the tool.

## Added

- **Continuous integration.** The suite runs on Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. `pyproject.toml` declares `requires-python = ">=3.11"` while development happens on 3.14, so three of those four versions were a promise nothing had tested. CI also runs the installed `secscan` console script (an entry point can be misdeclared while every in-process unit test passes) and pins both exit codes from D14: a missing path exits 2, a scan with findings exits 1.
- **The PyGoat sample report is now in the repository**, at `docs/sample-report.pdf` — a 33-page assessment — together with the three scripts and the markdown that build it, under `tools/report/`, with the two-step build documented. Those scripts were previously untracked, which left the PDF a binary with no reproducible source. The assessor address on the cover and sign-off was replaced with a neutral one.
- **A README section stating who may run this, above the install steps.** The authorization rule was previously described only in the section about `--active`, two thirds of the way down, which a reader skimming for install instructions would never reach — and the default passive mode also makes real requests to the target. The missing license line was added at the same time.

## Changed

- `decisions.md` D12 and D18 said the tool "will automatically apply" safe fixes after confirmation. There is no apply layer: no `--fix`, no `--apply`, and no code that edits a target file. What ships is the eligibility rule — `Fix.apply_safe`, enforced in `core/fix.py.__post_init__`, which refuses to mark a code patch safe regardless of caller. The entries now describe that instead.
- The status line at the top of `decisions.md` said the project was "building v1 foundation" with two model classes, and had said so since before v1.0.0 shipped. The README sends readers to that file first, so it was the first fact anyone learned about a finished tool. It is corrected, with a note on why a status line is the one kind of sentence a decisions log cannot carry unmaintained.
- `tools/report/README.md` claimed the print chain reproduces the committed PDF byte for byte. Run twice and compared, exactly eight bytes differ, all inside `/CreationDate` and `/ModDate`. The README now says that, with the snippet to check it.
- CI actions moved off the deprecated Node 20 runtimes (`actions/checkout` v4 to v7, `actions/setup-python` v5 to v7).

## Notes

- Coverage findings are all INFO severity and CONFIRMED confidence. The severity threshold gates the exit code only, so they appear in the report without turning a build red — a limitation of the scanner is not a vulnerability in your project.
- Coverage and vulnerability lookup are separate checks, so an OSV.dev outage cannot also erase the record of which manifests went unread.
- The test suite is 355 tests at this tag, up from 339 at v1.0.0. There is no network-blocking step in CI, deliberately: the claim that no test touches the network holds, but `pytest-socket` cannot prove it, because on Windows `asyncio.run()` builds a ProactorEventLoop that opens a socket for its own wakeup, and `--disable-socket` fails 115 tests that never go near a host. A check that fails for the wrong reason is worse than no check. (v1.2.0 does add that pass, with loopback allowed for exactly that reason.)
- Still true of this version: there is no apply layer, so every fix is something you make yourself.
- **Superseded by v1.1.1.** This tag was cut before the fix that stops the SAST walk descending into `venv/` and `__pycache__/`, so a default scan here reports findings in your dependencies' source. If you are picking a version, pick v1.1.1 or later.

## Install

From a clone, as documented in the README:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate       # on Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e .
```

That provides the `secscan` command. Without installing:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m scanner.cli path/to/code
```

Run it only against systems you own or have written permission to test. The default mode makes real requests to the target; `--active` sends attack-shaped input and additionally requires `--i-am-authorized`.

name: v1.0.0 — first release
body:
secscan takes one argument — a URL or a directory — and selects its own checks from what it was pointed at. A URL gets the web checks, a directory gets the code checks. This is the first tagged release, so there is no previous version to compare against; what follows is what the tool is. The v1 scope is SCA, SAST and DAST behind a single HTTP choke point, with an optional AI advisor that is off unless asked for.

## What it checks

- **SCA** — reads `requirements.txt` and `pyproject.toml` (PyPI) and `package.json` and `package-lock.json` (npm), queries OSV, and raises one finding per real-world flaw: OSV returns a record per source database, so a single CVE arriving as a GHSA *and* a PYSEC record is merged into one finding rather than reported twice. Severity comes from the advisory's CVSS vector, falling back to the database's own qualitative rating and then to HIGH, because an advisory with no severity attached is not an advisory to quietly treat as minor. A dependency is only queried when its version is exact; a range or unpinned entry is never guessed at, because a guessed version produces a finding about software you may not be running. In this release such an entry is simply not queried and does not appear in the report — surfacing it as explicitly unchecked is not in v1.0.0, and is the main thing v1.1.0 is for.
- **SAST** — walks a source tree against 17 rules: 10 dangerous-sink rules (`eval`, `shell=True`, and similar) and 7 hardcoded-credential rules. The one generic high-entropy-assignment rule is guarded by an entropy floor and a placeholder filter, so `api_key = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"` is not a finding. The six fixed-format rules (AWS, GitHub, Google, Slack, JWT, private key) are deliberately trusted by format alone — suppressing one for low entropy would be a false negative on a real leaked credential — so a documentation example of a real key shape, AWS's own published `AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE` included, will be reported.
- **DAST, passive** — TLS configuration, security headers, cookie flags, exposed files, and server fingerprinting, read from responses without tampering with them. This is the default behaviour.
- **DAST, active** — SQL injection and reflected XSS. Off unless `--active` and `--i-am-authorized` are both given and the host is in the active allowlist, which `--active` grants for an explicitly typed URL target; the engine additionally requires `dast.active.enabled`. Every one of those conditions is required and the defaults are fail-closed. The payloads detect rather than exploit: the XSS probe is a non-executing marker string that the check looks for in the response.
- **AI advisor** — optional and off by default. It reasons only over findings the deterministic scanners already produced, and attaches its advice as a `MANUAL` fix, which the `Fix` model refuses to let anything mark auto-applyable.

Reports render as terminal text, JSON, or HTML. The run exits `0` when nothing is at or above the severity threshold (default `medium`), `1` when something is, and `2` when the scan itself failed. The third case exists so that "found nothing" and "could not run" are not the same exit code in a pipeline.

## Safety properties, and where they are enforced

These are enforced in one place each rather than at every call site, so no individual scanner can forget them.

- **One HTTP choke point, two independent default-deny allowlists.** Every outbound request passes `AsyncHttpClient.request`, which permits a host only if it is in the target `Scope` (hosts you said you may scan) or in the egress allowlist (the four hosts the tool needs for its own operation: `api.osv.dev`, `pypi.org`, `registry.npmjs.org`, `api.anthropic.com`). Everything else is refused. The TLS probe is the one path that opens a raw socket instead of going through the client, because httpx does not expose a peer certificate; it takes the gate as a required positional argument and accepts only a target-scope verdict, refusing the egress hosts the client itself would allow. That was not true until shortly before this tag — see the last item under *Fixed*.
- **Credentials are scrubbed when a `Finding` is constructed, not when a report is written.** `Finding.__post_init__` scrubs and caps evidence, and the token shapes live in `core/redaction.py` rather than in the SAST rule pack, so core can enforce its own contract without importing a scanner. Writing it at the output layer would mean every current and future output path had to remember to.
- **A failed lookup is never reported as an absence of findings.** A non-2xx from OSV raises and surfaces as a recorded scan error in all three report formats, rather than deserializing to an empty vulnerability list.
- **The AI vendor SDK is deliberately not a dependency.** The advisor reaches the API over the same shared httpx client as everything else; an SDK with its own transport would be a way around the choke point. `lxml` is likewise absent: `beautifulsoup4` is a declared dependency and is what the crawler imports, but it is pointed at the standard library's `html.parser` backend, so the C-extension build was install cost for nothing. Both absences are documented in `pyproject.toml` so they are not "fixed" later by accident.

## Installing and running

Python 3.11 or newer. There is no PyPI package for this release; install from a clone.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e .
```

That installs a `secscan` command:

```bash
secscan path/to/code
secscan https://example.com
secscan path/to/code --format json
secscan path/to/code --format html --output report.html
secscan path/to/code --ai                       # needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
secscan https://your-own-site.com --active --i-am-authorized
```

Without installing:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m scanner.cli path/to/code
```

## Fixed before the tag

The unified core landed first and was live-verified against real targets and the real OSV database. Five defects that verification exposed were closed before tagging:

- **SCA was correct but slow.** The client screened with `/v1/querybatch` and then fetched every distinct advisory individually by id, sequentially. It now uses the batch call only to learn which packages are affected and then fetches full records with one concurrent `/v1/query` per affected package, so cost is `1 + (affected packages)` instead of `1 + (distinct vulnerabilities)`. Measured against live OSV on a project with 7 outdated packages: 181 requests dropped to 8 and 2m15s to 8.3s, with a byte-identical set of 75 findings. The batch screen was kept rather than replaced by per-package queries, which would cost one request per dependency even when nothing is vulnerable.
- **An OSV outage produced a clean report.** Every response body was read as data, so any non-2xx deserialized to `{}` and read as "no vulnerabilities". The status check lives in the OSV client and not in the shared HTTP client on purpose: DAST reads 4xx and 5xx as signal, and a 404 is the entire answer for exposed-file probing.
- **SQL injection evidence quoted the response body.** The pages this check fires on are the pages that print their failing query, so the finding could carry that query's parameters — an address, a session id, a token — into report files and into AI request bodies. Signatures are now grouped by database engine and the evidence names the engine only. Triage needs to know which database complained; it never needed the target's bytes to learn that.
- **Two SAST rules could contradict each other on one line.** Redaction is decided per rule — secret rules mask the matched value, sink rules quote the offending source line, which is what makes a sink finding actionable — but every rule is tried against every line, so a secret rule could mask a token while a sink rule on the same line printed it in full. `os.system` and `shell=True` lines are exactly where an inline `curl` with an auth header appears. The sink branch now scrubs before truncating, in that order, because truncating first leaves a token fragment that matches no shape and can never be scrubbed afterwards.
- **The tool's one raw socket asserted a scope check nothing performed.** `fetch_tls` opens an ssl handshake outside `AsyncHttpClient.request`, and both `core/http.py` and §9 of the integration contract stated as settled fact that it reused the gate to apply the same scope check. Neither was true of the code: the signature was `fetch_tls(url, *, timeout)` — no gate, no scope check, and no way to perform one. Nothing was exploitable, because the only caller passes the host `Scope` was seeded from, but the guarantee rested on nothing. The gate is now a required positional argument, so omitting it is a `TypeError` rather than a silently ungated probe, and the probe accepts only a TARGET verdict, refusing the egress hosts the shared client would allow.

A `LICENSE` file was also added. `pyproject.toml` had declared `license = { text = "MIT" }` from the start, but no license text was being distributed with the code.

## Known limits in this release

- Redaction matches fixed-format token families, never an entropy heuristic, because an entropy heuristic would mask certificate fingerprints and content hashes. A shapeless password such as `mysql -pHunter2` still appears in a finding. This is stated in the matcher rather than left for you to discover.
- The scrub at construction guards one of the fields that carry target-derived text, and `Finding` is not frozen, so this reduces credential amplification rather than removing it. An adversarial review of that change returned an unfavourable verdict and it is recorded in `decisions.md` as D44 rather than hidden; moving enforcement to the interpolation point is the next step.
- The evidence cap truncates visibly instead of raising. Evidence length is chosen by whatever a target sent, and aborting a scan over a verbose server would be a denial of service against the operator.
- SCA covers the four manifest formats listed above. Poetry and Pipfile lockfiles are not parsed in v1. In this release an unrecognized manifest produces no finding and no error — the SCA section simply looks the way a clean project's does, which is what v1.1.0 exists to fix.
- Active checks are SQL injection and reflected XSS only.
